newsitem.title: PERU: Peru wages musical war on Marxist guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Peru wages musical war on Marxist guerrillas.

text.p: Peru blasted military tunes at the Japanese ambassador's home on Tuesday to drown out revolutionary anthems played by Marxist rebels holding 72 VIP hostages and unnerve the guerrillas.
Shortly after dawn on the 42nd day of the crisis, police blared march music for half an hour from three sets of speakers placed around the mined and booby-trapped diplomatic compound.
The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas responded by playing their rebel hymn, but this was quickly muffled by the police's own recordings.
The musical battle lasted about 10 minutes and was repeated several hours later, with police again managing to obliterate the sound of the MRTA's hymn.
The activity followed Monday's display of strength by police, which drew the first direct shots at security forces since the brief shootout following the rebels' Dec. 17 takeover of the residence.
The increasingly bold police tactics heightened alarm in Tokyo, which is particularly concerned about two dozen Japanese nationals held captive.
Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto again called on Peru on Tuesday to tone down troop movements at the site.

"We understand the need to tighten security at the compound but ask that you give sufficient consideration to preventing accidents or incidents," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama quoted Hashimoto as telling President Alberto Fujimori by phone.
The spokesman declined to reveal the response of Fujimori, who he said called Hashimoto to explain Lima's stance.

The MRTA rebels fired several bullets on Monday at police aboard a convoy of armoured cars after officers made obscene gestures toward the residence while parading by. The bullets hit the vehicle, with one narrowly missing a policeman inside.
Even after the shooting, security forces, who had orders not to return fire, continued their manoeuvres in an apparent attempt to crack the resolve of the estimated 15 rebels.
About 200 special forces officers and four armoured vehicles paraded five times around the diplomatic compound while a police helicopter circled overhead.
Police have thrown stones and garbage into the diplomatic compound, flown helicopters overhead and trained machine guns on the house, moves the guerrillas considered a provocation.
Police kept their distance from the residence on Tuesday while Red Cross workers on bicycles took away scores of bags of rubbish put outside by the rebels.
Fujimori, whose brother Pedro is among the captives, has insisted the police moves are not a prelude to an assault but a tightening of security prior to talks and a negotiated exit.

Fujimori's point man in the crisis, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, said a site had been selected for eventual negotiations to end the six-week standoff and a bullet proof vehicle was ready to take MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini to the talks.
And in an apparent goodwill gesture, Palermo told a news conference that Catholic clergymen would form part of a commission to ensure jailed MRTA rebels are fairly treated.

A communique from MRTA prisoners in Lima's Canto Grande prison, sent on Tuesday to Reuters, slammed Fujimori's decision earlier this month to suspend family and Red Cross visits as "arbitrary and abusive."
It also denounced "harassment" from police making plans to to transfer them "as a pretext for a massacre of prisoners once the government decides to enter the residence by force."
Efforts to start talks between the MRTA and Palermo have stalled over the main rebel demand of freedom for about 400 jailed comrades which Fujimori has refused to discuss.
Local media reported on Tuesday that police had captured an important leader of the larger Shining Path guerrilla movement in Peru's northern coastal region.

Anti-terrorism police arrested Ciro Carranza in the city of Trujillo, 350 miles (560 km) north of Lima, on Saturday after he was discovered with false identification papers and coded messages, local newspapers said.
Conflicts unleashed by the MRTA and Shining Path have cost at least 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage in Peru since 1980.
